page: Vultr voc-c-16c-32gb-500s-amd is a compute-oriented virtual server instance belonging to the Optimized Cloud Compute family. Powered by an x86_64 AMD EPYC processor clocked at 2.0 GHz, the instance delivers 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled. The CPU configuration features 32 KB of L1 data cache, 0.5 MB of L2 cache, and 16 MB of L3 cache, with hardware support for AVX, AES, and SHA-NI instruction sets, though modern vector extensions such as AVX-512 and AMX are absent.

The hardware configuration pairs these 16 dedicated compute threads with 32.0 GB of system memory, establishing a 1:2 memory-to-vCPU ratio of 2.0 GB per thread. Storage is locally provisioned through a bundled 500 GB NVMe SSD, delivering low-latency local disk input and output without relying solely on remote network-attached volumes. Networking features a single complimentary public IPv4 address. Accelerated computing is not supported on this instance profile, as it contains zero GPUs.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong single-core compute performance, with stress-ng single-core execution reaching the top 10 percent of recorded results. Multi-core execution and overall PassMark CPU scores sit solidly within the middle 50 percent, reflecting standard throughput for an AMD EPYC platform running at a 2.0 GHz base frequency. In real-world application testing, the instance achieved 10,901 points in multi-core Geekbench testing, sustained 30.95 million operations per second on Redis SET workloads, and delivered 16.98 GB/sec in static web serving throughput. Small-model LLM text generation also landed in the upper quartile, generating 295.34 tokens per second.

From an architectural standpoint, the 1:2 RAM-to-vCPU allocation creates an efficient cost-performance profile for computational processing where large in-memory working sets are unnecessary. However, memory-intensive workloads may encounter capacity bottlenecks given the modest 32 GB pool across 16 active execution threads. This instance profile is best suited for continuous integration and build systems, multi-threaded code compilation, static web serving clusters, Redis caching layers, and compute-focused microservices.
